extracted.intended_audience: Washington Post journalists, editors, and newsroom staff (also relevant to contributors and readers seeking to understand editorial policies)
extracted.subtask_description: Editorial, ethical, sourcing, verification, corrections, and audience-engagement standards that govern how The Washington Post reporters and editors gather, verify, attribute, publish, correct and engage with readers. This is the organization's internal guidance and public statement of newsroom norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: The first mission of a newspaper
rubrics_metrics.description: The first mission of a newspaper is to tell the truth as nearly as the truth may be ascertained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of the Seven Principles for the Conduct of a Newspaper (Eugene Meyer, March 5, 1935). Sets the foundational obligation to pursue truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tell ALL the truth so far as it can learn it
rubrics_metrics.description: The newspaper shall tell ALL the truth so far as it can learn it, concerning the important affairs of America and the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes comprehensiveness about significant public affairs; part of the Seven Principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe the decencies obligatory upon a private gentleman
rubrics_metrics.description: As a disseminator of the news, the paper shall observe the decencies that are obligatory upon a private gentleman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A standard about tone and decorum in reporting; part of the Seven Principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fit reading for the young as well as for the old
rubrics_metrics.description: What it prints shall be fit reading for the young as well as for the old.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider audience sensibilities across ages when publishing; part of the Seven Principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to readers and the public, not owners' private interests
rubrics_metrics.description: The newspaper’s duty is to its readers and to the public at large, and not to the private interests of its owners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affirms editorial independence from owners' private interests; part of the Seven Principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be prepared to sacrifice material fortunes for the public good
rubrics_metrics.description: In the pursuit of truth, the newspaper shall be prepared to make sacrifices of its material fortunes, if such course be necessary for the public good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial choices may require financial cost to uphold public-interest reporting; part of the Seven Principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not ally with any special interest; be fair and free
rubrics_metrics.description: The newspaper shall not be the ally of any special interest, but shall be fair and free and wholesome in its outlook on public affairs and public men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid special-interest alignment; maintain fairness and independence; part of the Seven Principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics policy — living document
rubrics_metrics.description: These policies are meant to guide Washington Post journalism ... a 'living document' that we will continually modify and update based on feedback ... These guidelines should not be understood as establishing hard and fast rules or as covering every situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use judgment; consult editors; policies are guidance not absolute rules because circumstances vary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict of Interest
rubrics_metrics.description: This news organization is pledged to avoid conflicts of interest or the appearance of conflict of interest wherever and whenever possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key rules and examples: reporters pay their own way; accept no gifts or free trips; no free admission to non-public events except limited exceptions (press box, critic review); do not accept payment/honoraria/expenses from governments or organizations covered; avoid money from entities that lobby or influence issues covered; avoid active partisan involvement; disclose household/business ties that could appear compromising; avoid entanglements with likely subjects of interest. Exceptions are few and should be obvious; consult editors/legal when in doubt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters and editors of The Post are committed to fairness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fairness includes completeness (do not omit major facts), relevance (avoid irrelevant detail that displaces significant facts), honesty (avoid misleading the reader), and diligent seeking of comment from individuals/organizations covered and taking that comment genuinely into account. No story is fair if it omits facts of major importance or fails to give subjects opportunity to address claims about them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste
rubrics_metrics.description: The Washington Post respects taste and decency ... We shall avoid prurience. We shall avoid profanities and obscenities unless their use is so essential to a story of significance that its meaning is lost without them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obscenities require approval from executive or managing editors. If potentially offensive material has legitimate news value, include visual/text warnings. Do not link to sites that aid or abet illegal activity without Legal Department consultation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opinion/news separation and labeling
rubrics_metrics.description: The separation of news columns from the editorial pages is solemn and complete ... honest, in-depth reporting, or analysis or commentary when plainly labeled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Labels and definitions: Analysis (interpretation based on evidence), Perspective (discussion with a point of view, including first-person narratives), Opinion (columns/blogs in Opinions section), Review (professional critic’s assessment). Ensure labeling is clear when analysis/commentary appears in news contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social media conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: When using networks such as Facebook, Twitter etc., for reporting or for our personal lives, we must protect our professional integrity ... Washington Post journalists are always Washington Post journalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social-media accounts reflect on the newsroom; consider every comment/link public regardless of privacy settings; refrain from posting anything that could objectively be perceived as reflecting political, racial, sexist, religious or other bias or favoritism.

rubrics_metrics.name: National and Community Interest
rubrics_metrics.description: The Washington Post is vitally concerned with the national interest and with the community interest ... The claim of national interest by a federal official does not automatically equate with the national interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess claims of national or community interest critically rather than accepting official assertions at face value.

rubrics_metrics.name: A journalist's role — be stagehand not star
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters should make every effort to remain in the audience, to be the stagehand rather than the star, to report the news, not to make the news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not misrepresent identity or occupation; do not portray yourself as police, physicians, etc.; reporting should be honorable and explainable publicly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification and fact-checking standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Washington Post reporters have primary responsibility for reporting, writing, and fact-checking their stories. Stories are subject to review by one or more editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multi-level review structure: assignment editors (origination & initial review), multiplatform/copy editors (initial review for breaking news; second-level review for other stories), and senior editors (overall oversight). Number/extent of editor review varies with complexity, sensitivity, and time pressure. Digital-presentation editors may also be involved. Reporters remain primarily responsible but should collaborate with editors on verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Diversity is at the core of Washington Post journalism ... engaging a variety of voices as interviewees and first-person writers, striving for a staff that reflects a range of backgrounds and life experiences, and seeking feedback from all who would give it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Post submits staff diversity data to the American Society of News Editors; reporters ought to seek new specialists and a broad range of voices in stories (including women, people of color, younger people, unconventional thinkers, and affected ordinary citizens).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ownership transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Ownership structure: The Washington Post is owned by Jeffrey P. Bezos ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publicly disclose ownership; maintain editorial independence despite ownership. (Page states owner and founding date.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrections policy — general
rubrics_metrics.description: The Washington Post strives for a nimble, accurate and complete news report. We endeavor to be promptly responsive in correcting errors ... When we run a correction, clarification or editor’s note, our goal is to tell readers, as clearly and quickly as possible, what was wrong and what is correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use clear, prompt notices understandable to readers. It is unnecessary to put notes on stories stating they have been updated unless new information/change warrants note; time stamp signals developing story. Use correction/clarification/editor’s note when appropriate (see detailed subrules).

rubrics_metrics.name: Updating a digital report
rubrics_metrics.description: Our individual pieces of journalism evolve as we sharpen and improve them ... The time stamp signals to readers that they are reading a developing story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not add update notes to every edit; add a correction/clarification/editor's note whenever a significant mistake is corrected or when there is particular reason to note new information or other change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrections vs Clarifications vs Editor's Notes
rubrics_metrics.description: Corrections: publish a correction explaining the change when substantively correcting content. Clarification: language rewritten and a clarification added when facts are correct but language was unclear. Editor’s Notes: used when a correction calls into question entire substance of an article or raises significant ethical matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editor’s Notes require senior-editor approval. Clarifications also used to note belatedly added comments/response or new reporting that shifts account. Apply appropriate label depending on nature and gravity of the issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other corrections practices
rubrics_metrics.description: If an error is found by a reader and posted to the comment stream, the audience engagement team should indicate in comments that it has been corrected. If incorrect information was sent in an alert, send an alert informing people that the earlier alert was wrong and provide accurate information. When we publish erroneous information on social networks, we should correct it on that platform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attribute blame to individual reporters or editors; may note if error resulted from production problem or a trusted source. Ensure corrections applied across platforms (site, alerts, social).

rubrics_metrics.name: Take-down (unpublish) requests
rubrics_metrics.description: As a matter of editorial policy, we do not grant take-down requests, which should be vetted at the highest level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a subject claims inaccuracy, investigate and, if necessary, publish a correction; consider updates or follow-up coverage rather than removing article. Take-downs considered only in exceptional circumstances (e.g., person under threat of physical harm because of the existence of the material).

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy on sources — transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: The Washington Post is committed to disclosing to its readers the sources of the information in its stories to the maximum possible extent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for transparency so readers know how/where information was obtained; transparency is tied to honesty and fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidential sources
rubrics_metrics.description: When we use an unnamed source, we are asking our readers to take an extra step to trust the credibility of the information ... Granting anonymity to a source should not be done casually or automatically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer named sources; prefer at least two independent sources for confidential information with firsthand knowledge; a relevant document can sometimes serve as second source. Use of a single source permitted only after deliberations involving executive editor, managing editor and appropriate department head and depends on source reliability and basis for information. Editors must know identities of unnamed sources; resist when a source asks reporter not to tell editors. Explain to readers why unnamed sources deserve confidence (give readers more specific attributions than generic 'sources').

rubrics_metrics.name: Dealing with sources
rubrics_metrics.description: We strive to treat sources fairly ... Potentially controversial statements should be quoted in a complete sentence or paragraph when possible, and in context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give subjects reasonable opportunity to respond and avoid last-minute calls if avoidable; do not promise sources that reporting will cease; avoid ad hominem quotations from unnamed sources; avoid blind quotations; do not use pseudonyms or mislead about identities; decisions to use less than full names must involve editors and explanation to readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution and original reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: We must be truthful about the source of our information. Facts and quotations not produced by our own reporting must be attributed. Plagiarism is not permitted. The Post places a premium on original reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make clear when reporter was not present at a scene; reconstructive narrative based on witnesses must include attribution; discuss special attribution problems with editors; credit significant reporting by stringers or other staff in byline/tagline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground rules and attribution definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions: On the record (attributable by name); On background / not for attribution (attributable to a described source, not named); Deep background (included but not attributed — to be avoided if possible); Off the record (information cannot be used for publication or further reporting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start interviews presuming on the record; clarify terms before interviews that are not on the record; prefer on-the-record interviews; avoid deep background and off-the-record information because they limit transparency; explain and document ground rules (preferably on tape) and have editors involved in decisions about nonstandard attribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quoting sources and sharing material with sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective is to capture people's words and intended meaning accurately. We do not allow sources to change the rules governing specific quotations after the fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not allow sources to change original quotes; permitting addition to a quotation can be an alternative but must be explained to readers. Sharing sections of stories with sources for technical accuracy may be acceptable; sharing entire drafts is prohibited except with rare, high-level permission. Reporters should not make promises or agreements incompatible with policy and standards; be prepared for communications to become public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert sources — diversify and broaden voices
rubrics_metrics.description: We quote many people and rely on experts for context, but must think about who we are quoting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid dependence on same academics/public figures; seek new specialists and voices (women, younger people, people of color, unconventional thinkers) and include ordinary people affected by events to better reflect readership and population.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader engagement and feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: The Post welcomes reader contributions; nearly all articles offer comment sections and reporters/editors are encouraged to participate in comments according to their preference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask commenters to keep tone civil and follow Discussion and Submission Guidelines; 24/7 moderation team handles offensive comments; audience engagement team should note corrections in comment streams; provide channels for letters to the editor, op-ed submissions, live chats, and contacts (Help Center, reader representative).
